about: Definitions of serendipity, worked out from core codes. A coder never ticks a definition: the coding page and the analysis mark an episode as meeting a definition when every code it needs is ticked. Sentences are copied from the papers' passages (chosen by reading, 23 Oct 2026).

evidence.text: Based on the three necessary conditions that I derived from the review (agency, surprise, and value), I define serendipity as ‘surprising discovery that results from unplanned moments in which our decisions and actions lead to valuable outcomes’.
In a recent review, Busch (2024) identified three necessary conditions that distinguish serendipity from related concepts.

In contrast to pure luck, Busch (2024) argues that in addition to the necessary conditions of surprise and value forming luck, respectively, agency is a third necessary condition for serendipity to happen.
Serendipity involves the convergence of agency, surprise, and value ( Busch, 2024 ), and implies purposeful action in response to unforeseen cues ( Busch and Barkema, 2022 ; Rauch and Ansari, 2022 ).
Value, together with agency and surprise, is one of the necessary conditions of serendipity (Busch, 2024).
Recent work frames serendipity as the interplay of unexpectedness, agency, and value ( Busch, 2024 ; Busch and Grimes, 2023 ).
In essence, serendipity involves the interaction of three elements: a resource (sagacity), an event (contingencies), and an activity (the individual is already on a journey).
Serendipity is conceptualized as the combination of search (directed effort), contingency (favourable accidents), and prior knowledge (sagacity).

Because serendipity is characterized by “some combination of search (directed effort), contingency (favorable accidents) and prior knowledge (sagacity) ” (Dew, 2009 : 736), attracting stakeholders' pre-commitments and enlarging the means available to the venture serves to enhance the pool of knowledge required to detect and act on key contingencies.

Dew (2009, p. 739) suggests that serendipity “involves the interaction of three elements (i) a resource (sagacity), (ii) an event (contingency), (iii) an activity (the individual is already on a journey).
Entrepreneurial serendipity also contains the three elements of serendipity from Dew’s (2009) conceptual model: knowledge, search and contingency.

Defined in the management literature as a “ search leading to unintended discovery ” ( Dew, 2009 , p. 735), serendipity is more than mere chance, arising from the interplay of searching, contingency, and prior knowledge ( Dew, 2009 ).

Horace Walpole, who coined the word, said in a letter of Jan. 28, 1754, that he took it from the title of a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip; the princes “were always making discoveries by accident and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of.”

Chute calls sortes Walpolianae,” for, whether sortes is translated as “luck” or “fate,” it lacks the mixture of those two ingredients that Walpole irrevocably included in the complex meaning of serendipity: accident and sagacity.
We define serendipity as entrepreneurs “making discoveries, by accidents and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of” (Merton & Barber, 2004, p. 2).

In his letter to his diplomatist friend Walpole mentioned a special type of luck that these princes bestow: he termed it serendipity, after the ancient tale, which resulted from the combination of an accident with sagacity or perspicacity in understanding.
Serendipity in finding and exploring new things is, however, believed to be a result of “accident and sagacity”, rather than accident or luck alone ( Friedel, 2001 ).

Referencing the Persian fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip, Horace Walpole described serendipity as “making discoveries, by accident and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of” (quoted in Merton and Barber, 2004).
He refers to serendipity as an unexpected discovery found from the combination of accident and sagacity ( Rosenman, 2001 ).
Columbus’ discovery of the ‘New World’ was, of course, an example of serendipity: of making a discovery, by accident and sagacity, of things not in quest of.
